## Why the within estimator breaks

A firm does not jump to the workforce it wants. Hiring takes months and
firing costs money, so this year's employment is last year's employment
moved part of the way toward a target set by wages, capital and demand.
Put last year's outcome on the right-hand side and the panel regression is
**dynamic**:

$$
y_{it} = \gamma\, y_{i,t-1} + x_{it}'\beta + \alpha_i + \varepsilon_{it},
\qquad i = 1, \dots, N;\ t = 2, \dots, T,
$$

with $\alpha_i$ the firm effect and $\varepsilon_{it}$ an innovation that
is serially uncorrelated and uncorrelated with $\alpha_i$ [@baltagi2021,
eqs. 8.1–8.2; @croissant2019, sec. 7.1]. The coefficient γ is the
**persistence** of the outcome: how much of last year survives into this
year. The 140 UK firms of @arellano1991, observed 1976–1984, are the panel
on which every method in this note was first run, and the benchmark data
set of Stata and EViews [@baltagi2021, p. 193; @croissant2019, p. 183].

Two things go wrong at once. The effect $\alpha_i$ is in every period's
$y$, so it is in $y_{i,t-1}$ too: the lagged outcome is correlated with
the error, and pooled OLS is biased upward, by an amount that vanishes
only when $\sigma^2_\alpha$ does [@baltagi2021, p. 187; @croissant2019,
pp. 163–164]. The obvious cure is the within transformation of the
[core chapter](../05-core/index.qmd#sec-core-fe-re), which subtracts each
firm's mean and so removes $\alpha_i$. It trades one correlation for
another. The demeaned lag $y_{i,t-1} - \bar y_{i,-1}$ contains every
period's $y$ and hence every period's $\varepsilon$; the demeaned error
$\varepsilon_{it} - \bar\varepsilon_i$ contains every period's
$\varepsilon$ as well, among them the $\varepsilon_{i,t-1}$ that sits
inside $y_{i,t-1}$. The two share a term in every period, and the sum of
those shared terms is the **Nickell bias**: of order $1/T$, so it does not
shrink as more firms are added, only as more years are [@nickell1981;
@baltagi2021, p. 188; @croissant2019, p. 165]. It is a bias of demeaning,
not of the fixed-effects assumption: random-effects GLS quasi-demeans and
is biased the same way [@pesaran2015, p. 678].

The size of it is known exactly. For the pure autoregression with no
regressors, @pesaran2015 [eqs. 27.7–27.11] takes the large-$N$ limit of
the within estimator from the moments of the demeaned lag. In the form
@croissant2019 [p. 165] print, with $T$ the number of periods in the
regression once one lag is taken and
$A = 1 - (1 - \gamma^{T}) / \{T(1 - \gamma)\}$,

$$
\operatorname*{plim}_{N \to \infty}\,(\hat\gamma_{FE} - \gamma)
= -\,\frac{1 + \gamma}{T - 1}\;
  \frac{A}{1 - \dfrac{2\gamma A}{(1 - \gamma)(T - 1)}} .
$$

Compactly, the limit is $-(1 + \gamma)/T + O(T^{-2})$: negative for
$\gamma \geq 0$, equal to $-1/T$ at $\gamma = 0$, and large when $T$ is
in the 3 to 8 range typical of household and firm panels [@pesaran2015,
pp. 679–680]. At $\gamma = 0.5$ and $T = 10$, which CM call "a fairly long
time span", the bias is $-0.167$: a third of the coefficient
[@croissant2019, p. 165]. Longer panels do not make it safe. In the Monte
Carlo of @judson1999, with $N = 20$ or $100$ and $T$ up to 30, the bias
grows with γ, falls with $T$, and even at $T = 30$ can still be 20 % of
the true value [@baltagi2021, p. 188]. The within estimator is consistent
only as $T \to \infty$ [@baltagi2021, p. 188].

Two numbers bracket the truth. OLS is biased up, within is biased down,
so any consistent estimator should land between them [@croissant2019,
p. 168]. The bias step draws exactly that picture. Three ways out exist:
correct the within estimator for its known bias [@kiviet1995;
@baltagi2021, p. 188], write a likelihood that handles the initial
observation [@hsiao2002; @pesaran2015, sec. 27.6], or remove $\alpha_i$ by
a transformation that leaves a usable instrument behind. This note is
about the third.

## The minimum math

### Difference, then instrument

First differences remove the effect without averaging over time,

$$
\Delta y_{it} = \gamma\, \Delta y_{i,t-1} + \Delta x_{it}'\beta
  + \Delta\varepsilon_{it}, \qquad t = 3, \dots, T,
$$

and with it every time-invariant regressor [@baltagi2021, eq. 8.4 and
p. 192; @pesaran2015, eq. 27.19]. The lag is still endogenous:
$\Delta y_{i,t-1}$ contains $\varepsilon_{i,t-1}$ and
$\Delta\varepsilon_{it} = \varepsilon_{it} - \varepsilon_{i,t-1}$ contains
it with a minus sign, so
$E[\Delta y_{i,t-1}\Delta\varepsilon_{it}] = -\sigma^2_\varepsilon$ and
OLS on the differenced equation is inconsistent [@pesaran2015, p. 682]. The
differenced error is also a first-order moving average: its variance is
$2\sigma^2_\varepsilon$, its first autocovariance $-\sigma^2_\varepsilon$,
and all higher ones zero [@pesaran2015, p. 682; @croissant2019, p. 166].

An **instrument** is a variable correlated with the regressor that causes
trouble and uncorrelated with the error. @anderson1982 saw that $y_{i,t-2}$
is one: it is correlated with $\Delta y_{i,t-1}$, and it is uncorrelated
with $\Delta\varepsilon_{it}$ as long as the innovations themselves are
serially uncorrelated. The difference $\Delta y_{i,t-2}$ qualifies on the
same argument [@baltagi2021, p. 188; @pesaran2015, p. 682]. Between the
two, @arellano1989 found that the estimator on the differenced instrument
has a singularity point and very large variances over a significant range
of parameter values, while the one on the level has no singularity and much
smaller variances, and is the one to use [@baltagi2021, p. 188;
@croissant2019, p. 167]. The within transformation cannot take the place
of differencing here: its error $\varepsilon_{it} - \bar\varepsilon_i$
contains every realisation of $\varepsilon$, so no lag of $y$ is
uncorrelated with it [@croissant2019, p. 166]. (Orthogonal deviations,
each observation minus the mean of those after it, are the other
transformation that works, and lose one observation per gap instead of
two [@croissant2019, pp. 166–167].)

The instrument is not strong. With no regressors, $T = 3$, and the
innovations uncorrelated with $\alpha_i$ and with $y_{i0}$, the level
instrument has

$$
E[y_{i,t-2}\,\Delta y_{i,t-1}]
  = -\sigma^2_\varepsilon\,(1 - \gamma)\,
    \frac{1 - \gamma^{2(t-1)}}{1 - \gamma^2},
$$

non-zero for $|\gamma| < 1$ but shrinking toward zero as γ approaches one,
and the approach breaks down at $\gamma = 1$ [@pesaran2015, p. 682].
Anderson–Hsiao is consistent but not efficient, for two reasons: it uses
one instrument where several are valid, and it ignores the moving-average
structure of the differenced error [@baltagi2021, p. 188; @pesaran2015,
p. 682; @croissant2019, p. 168].

### Every lag is an instrument

@arellano1991 fixed both. In the first usable period, $t = 3$, the
equation $\Delta y_{i3} = \gamma \Delta y_{i2} + \Delta\varepsilon_{i3}$
has one valid instrument, $y_{i1}$. At $t = 4$ both $y_{i1}$ and $y_{i2}$
are uncorrelated with $\Delta\varepsilon_{i4}$; one more instrument
arrives with each period, until at $t = T$ the set is
$y_{i1}, \dots, y_{i,T-2}$ [@baltagi2021, pp. 189–190; @pesaran2015,
p. 683; @croissant2019, p. 168]. Stacked, the instruments of one firm
form the block-diagonal matrix

$$
W_i = \begin{pmatrix}
  [y_{i1}] & & & 0 \\
  & [y_{i1}, y_{i2}] & & \\
  & & \ddots & \\
  0 & & & [y_{i1}, \dots, y_{i,T-2}]
\end{pmatrix},
$$

one row per differenced period, and the claim that each block is
uncorrelated with its period's error is the set of **moment conditions**
$E(W_i'\Delta\varepsilon_i) = 0$ [@baltagi2021, eq. 8.6; @pesaran2015,
eqs. 27.27–27.28; @croissant2019, eq. 7.4]. @holtzeakin1988 and @ahn1995
stated the same conditions [@baltagi2021, p. 190]. Their number is
$\tfrac12(T-1)(T-2)$ for $T$ periods: 36 at $T = 10$, and it grows with
the square of $T$ [@croissant2019, p. 172].

The **generalised method of moments** (GMM) turns the conditions into an
estimator. Replace the expectation by the sample mean
$m(\theta) = N^{-1}\sum_i W_i'\Delta\varepsilon_i(\theta)$, and since
there are more conditions than parameters, choose θ to make
$m(\theta)'\,A\,m(\theta)$ as small as possible for a weighting matrix $A$
[@hansen1982; @croissant2019, eqs. 7.5–7.7]. The efficient weight is the
inverse of the covariance of the moments [@croissant2019, p. 169]. If the
innovations are homoskedastic and serially uncorrelated, that covariance
is known up to scale, because the differenced error of a firm has
$E(\Delta\varepsilon_i\Delta\varepsilon_i') = \sigma^2_\varepsilon G$ with
$G$ the $(T-2) \times (T-2)$ band matrix of 2 on the diagonal and $-1$
beside it [@baltagi2021, eq. 8.5; @pesaran2015, eq. 27.33;
@croissant2019, eq. 7.8]. Using $A = (\sum_i W_i' G W_i)^{-1}$ gives the
**one-step** estimator,

$$
\hat\gamma_1 = \big[\Delta y_{-1}' W (W'(I_N \otimes G)W)^{-1}
  W' \Delta y_{-1}\big]^{-1}
  \big[\Delta y_{-1}' W (W'(I_N \otimes G)W)^{-1} W' \Delta y\big],
$$

[@baltagi2021, eq. 8.8]. The **two-step** estimator replaces the assumed
covariance by one built from the one-step residuals,
$V_N = \sum_i W_i'\,\Delta\hat\varepsilon_i\Delta\hat\varepsilon_i'\,W_i$,

$$
\hat\gamma_2 = \big[\Delta y_{-1}' W V_N^{-1} W' \Delta y_{-1}\big]^{-1}
  \big[\Delta y_{-1}' W V_N^{-1} W' \Delta y\big],
\qquad
\widehat{\operatorname{var}}(\hat\gamma_2)
  = \big[\Delta y_{-1}' W V_N^{-1} W' \Delta y_{-1}\big]^{-1},
$$

which is the optimal GMM estimator of @hansen1982 for $N \to \infty$ at
fixed $T$, needs no assumption about the initial observations or the
distributions of $\alpha_i$ and $\varepsilon_{it}$, and is robust to
heteroskedasticity and serial correlation in the weight [@baltagi2021,
eqs. 8.9–8.10 and pp. 190–191; @croissant2019, p. 171]. The two steps are
asymptotically equivalent when the innovations are IID [@baltagi2021,
p. 191]. Regressors join on the same logic: a strictly exogenous
$x_{it}$ instruments itself, a predetermined one contributes its lags
$x_{i1}, \dots, x_{i,t-1}$ as further columns of $W_i$ [@pesaran2015,
pp. 683–685]. This is **difference GMM**.

### The system and its price

Difference GMM inherits the weakness of its instruments. Take the
autoregression with $T = 3$, where the single moment condition
$E(y_{i1}\Delta\varepsilon_{i3}) = 0$ just identifies γ and GMM is plain
two-stage least squares. The first stage regresses $\Delta y_{i2}$ on
$y_{i1}$, and the model says
$\Delta y_{i2} = (\gamma - 1)\,y_{i1} + \alpha_i + \varepsilon_{i2}$, so
with $c = (1 - \gamma)/(1 + \gamma)$ the first-stage coefficient has

$$
\operatorname{plim}\,\hat\pi = (\gamma - 1)\,
  \frac{c}{c + \sigma^2_\alpha / \sigma^2_\varepsilon} ,
$$

which is pulled toward zero as γ approaches one or as the effect variance
grows relative to the innovation variance; the first-stage $F$ converges
to a non-central $\chi^2_1$ whose non-centrality goes to zero as
$\gamma \to 1$ [@blundell1998; @baltagi2021, eqs. 8.33–8.35;
@croissant2019, eq. 7.19]. The series is nearly a unit root, the random
walk of the [time chapter](../04-time/index.qmd#sec-ur-why), and lagged
levels then say almost nothing about current changes. The estimator is
biased and imprecise, and @blundell1998 named the cause: **weak
instruments** [@baltagi2021, p. 201; @pesaran2015, p. 685].

@arellano1995 and @blundell1998 add a second equation. Keep the model in
levels, $y_{it} = \gamma y_{i,t-1} + \alpha_i + \varepsilon_{it}$, and
instrument $y_{i,t-1}$ with the lagged difference $\Delta y_{i,t-1}$,
which carries no $\alpha_i$. The moment conditions

$$
E\big[\Delta y_{i,t-1}\,(\alpha_i + \varepsilon_{it})\big] = 0,
\qquad t = 3, \dots, T,
$$

are $T - 2$ in number and not redundant given the difference conditions
[@baltagi2021, p. 202]; the longer lags $\Delta y_{i,t-s}$, $s \geq 2$,
would add nothing, since each is a combination of conditions already used
[@croissant2019, pp. 175–176]. Stacking the two sets of equations and the
two sets of instruments gives **system GMM**, which also estimates an
intercept [@croissant2019, p. 177]. Its price is an assumption about
where each firm started. The levels conditions hold if

$$
E\Big[\Big(y_{i1} - \frac{\alpha_i}{1 - \gamma}\Big)\alpha_i\Big] = 0 :
$$

the deviation of the first observation from the firm's long-run mean is
uncorrelated with the effect, so that from the second period on each
series converges toward its own mean [@baltagi2021, eq. 8.36;
@pesaran2015, eqs. 27.37–27.38]. @croissant2019 [p. 176] show that this
**initial-condition restriction** either holds in every period or in none,
and read it pragmatically: the deviation decays at rate γ, so a process
that started long ago is near its steady state and the condition is close
enough. Its validity is what the whole estimator rests on [@pesaran2015,
p. 689], which is why the Sargan test of the next section is best run on
the levels conditions alone as well as on the full set [@croissant2019,
p. 180].

What the extra equation buys is large when the instruments of the
difference equation are weak. For $T = 4$ and
$\sigma^2_\alpha / \sigma^2_\varepsilon = 1$, the asymptotic variance of
difference GMM divided by that of system GMM is 1.75 at $\gamma = 0$, 3.26
at $\gamma = 0.5$ and 55.4 at $\gamma = 0.9$ [@blundell1998; @baltagi2021,
p. 202]; the Monte Carlo of @blundell2000ifs finds the same in finite
samples, especially in the weak-instrument case [@pesaran2015, p. 689]. On
a production function for 509 US firms, difference GMM gave a low capital
coefficient with low precision and system GMM a reasonable one that did
not reject constant returns [@blundell2000; @baltagi2021, p. 202]. Two
cautions. @bun2010 show that system GMM keeps a weak-instrument problem of
its own: its bias and root mean squared error are smaller than difference
GMM's when the series is persistent, but both grow with
$\sigma^2_\alpha / \sigma^2_\varepsilon$ and can become substantial, and
its Wald test, already size-distorted for both estimators with persistent
data, deteriorates further as that ratio rises [@baltagi2021, p. 202]. And
the weakness itself depends on the initial condition: @hayakawa2009 shows
that when the initial condition leaves the series' mean non-stationary and
the effect variance is much larger than the innovation variance,
difference GMM has no weak-instrument problem at all [@baltagi2021,
p. 202].

## Reading the diagnostics

**Overidentification.** With more moment conditions than parameters, the
conditions GMM did not need to fit can be checked. The statistic of
@sargan1958, applied to GMM by @hansen1982, is the minimised objective of
the two-step estimator,

$$
S = \Delta\hat\varepsilon' W \Big(\sum_i W_i'
  \Delta\hat\varepsilon_i\Delta\hat\varepsilon_i' W_i\Big)^{-1}
  W' \Delta\hat\varepsilon \;\sim\; \chi^2_{J - K},
$$

with $J$ the number of instrument columns and $K$ the number of
coefficients, under the null that every moment condition holds
[@baltagi2021, p. 191; @pesaran2015, p. 691; @croissant2019, p. 180]. A
rejection says at least one instrument is correlated with the error. A
non-rejection says less than it seems. @bowsher2002 fixed $N = 100$ and
let $T$ run from 5 to 15 with the full Arellano–Bond instrument set. At
$T = 5$ the test behaves: size 0.052 at the 5 % level, power 0.742. At
$T = 15$ the $\chi^2_{90}$ statistic has Monte Carlo mean 91.3, close to
its theoretical 90, but Monte Carlo variance 13.7 against a theoretical
180, and the rejection rate is zero under the null and under the
alternative alike. The cause is a poorly estimated weighting matrix, not
weak instruments [@baltagi2021, p. 192; @pesaran2015, p. 691]. In applied
work the symptom is a $p$-value near one: @roodman2009note re-ran two
published growth regressions, and in one of them the test's $p$-value of
0.97 fell to 0.001 once the instrument set was cut [@croissant2019,
pp. 180–183].

**Serial correlation.** Everything above assumed the innovations are
serially uncorrelated, the property tested on static residuals in the
[core chapter](../05-core/index.qmd#sec-core-serial). Here it is the
condition that makes $y_{i,t-2}$ a valid instrument: consistency rests on
$E[\Delta\varepsilon_{it}\Delta\varepsilon_{i,t-2}] = 0$ [@baltagi2021,
p. 192; @pesaran2015, p. 685]. @arellano1991 test it on the differenced
residuals with the statistic

$$
m_l = \frac{a_l}{\sqrt{\hat b_l}}, \qquad
a_l = \frac{1}{\sqrt N}\,\Delta\hat\varepsilon'\,\Delta\hat\varepsilon_{-l},
$$

where $\Delta\hat\varepsilon_{-l}$ is the residual lagged $l$ periods and
$\hat b_l$ a variance that accounts for the estimated coefficients;
$m_l$ is standard normal under no serial correlation of order $l$
[@croissant2019, pp. 181–182]. The two orders read differently. Order one
must reject, because $\Delta\varepsilon_{it}$ and
$\Delta\varepsilon_{i,t-1}$ share $\varepsilon_{i,t-1}$ by construction.
Order two must not: $\Delta\varepsilon_{it}$ and
$\Delta\varepsilon_{i,t-2}$ are correlated only if $\varepsilon_{i,t-1}$
and $\varepsilon_{i,t-2}$ are, that is, if the innovations in levels are
serially correlated of order one, and then the instruments dated $t - 2$
fail [@baltagi2021, p. 192; @croissant2019, p. 182]. The null of $m_2$ is
also true if the innovations follow a random walk, in which case OLS on
the differenced model is consistent as well and @arellano1991 give a
Hausman-type test, a comparison of the two estimates, to tell the cases
apart [@baltagi2021, p. 192].

**Two-step standard errors.** The first Monte Carlo on the estimator, 100
replications with $N = 100$ and $T = 7$, found GMM nearly unbiased and
much more precise than Anderson–Hsiao, and its two-step standard errors
too small [@arellano1991; @baltagi2021, p. 193]. @windmeijer2005 traced
the shortfall to the weighting matrix: $V_N$ is built from one-step
residuals, so the two-step estimator is a nonlinear function of the data
through them, and the usual formula ignores that. A first-order expansion
of the estimator in the estimated weight gives the **Windmeijer
correction**, which adds to the conventional two-step covariance $V_2$
the terms $V_2 D' + D V_2 + D V_1 D'$, with $D$ the gradient of the
estimator with respect to the weight and $V_1$ the one-step covariance
[@croissant2019, eqs. 7.27–7.29]. The correction is accurate when all the
moment conditions are linear, as they are here; without it, Wald tests on
two-step estimates are oversized [@baltagi2021, p. 193]. The imprecision
is structural: the moment covariance has $J(J+1)/2$ free elements, each a
fourth-order moment of the data, estimated from $N$ firms
[@croissant2019, p. 178]. @bond2001 go one step further and test
hypotheses by the difference of two Sargan statistics instead of a Wald
statistic, with better size in their Monte Carlo [@baltagi2021, p. 193].

**Too many instruments.** The count $\tfrac12(T-1)(T-2)$ is only for the
lags of $y$; with $T = 10$ and five strictly exogenous regressors it
reaches 500 [@baltagi2021, p. 194]. @ziliak1997 asked whether the
bias–efficiency trade-off known from time series survives in panels with
hundreds of units, and found that it does: on 532 men over ten years, the
GMM estimate of the intertemporal substitution elasticity of labour supply
moved from 0.519 to 0.093 as the moment conditions went from 9 to 212,
while its standard error fell from 0.36 to 0.07. He attributed the
downward bias to the correlation between the sample moments and the
estimated weighting matrix, and recommended a sub-optimal instrument set
over the full one [@baltagi2021, p. 194]. The mechanism is overfitting:
the more instruments, the closer the first-stage fit, until with as many
instruments as observations the instrumental-variables estimator is OLS
[@croissant2019, p. 172; @roodman2009]. Two cuts are standard. Limit the
lag depth, which at $T = 10$ and three lags gives 21 instruments instead
of 36 [@croissant2019, pp. 172–173]. Or **collapse** the matrix, keeping one
column per lag distance instead of one per lag and period, so that the
$T - 2$ moments $\sum_t y_{i,t-2}\Delta\varepsilon_{it}$,
$\sum_t y_{i,t-3}\Delta\varepsilon_{it}, \dots$ replace the full block
diagonal [@roodman2009note; @croissant2019, eq. 7.18; @baltagi2021,
p. 194]. A result that holds across lag depths and under collapsing is
the result; one that moves with the instrument count, as Ziliak's did, is
not. Large $T$ brings its own version of the problem: as $T \to \infty$
the estimator stays asymptotically normal but carries a bias of order
$1/N$ unless $T/N \to 0$ [@pesaran2015, p. 685].

## Four notations

The three anchor texts and this book each write the model differently,
and the lag coefficient changes letter with each:

| Where | Lag coefficient | Effect and innovation |
|---|---|---|
| @baltagi2021 [eq. 8.1] | δ | $\mu_i + \nu_{it}$ |
| @pesaran2015 [eq. 27.1] | λ | $\alpha_i + u_{it}$ |
| @croissant2019 [sec. 7.1] | ρ | $\eta_n + \varepsilon_{nt}$ |
| this book | γ | $\alpha_i + \varepsilon_{it}$ |

Baltagi's $T$ counts the periods observed, Pesaran's the periods in the
regression after the initial observation, and this book follows the
latter, so that the bias formula above is read with $T$ equal to the
number of years that enter the regression. The estimators keep their
names across texts: difference GMM is Arellano–Bond, system GMM is
Blundell–Bond, and `pgmm` calls the first `transformation = "d"` and the
second `"ld"`; the steps own every other argument.

## If / then

| If | Then |
|---|---|
| The model has a lagged outcome and $T$ is short | The within slope on the lag is biased down by about $(1 + \gamma)/T$; do not read it as the persistence [@pesaran2015, p. 679; @baltagi2021, p. 188] |
| $T$ is 30 or less | The bias can still be 20 % of γ; use an instrumental estimator [@judson1999; @baltagi2021, p. 188] |
| OLS and within disagree on the lag | They should: OLS above, within below. A consistent estimate lands between them [@croissant2019, p. 168] |
| One instrument is enough | Use the level $y_{i,t-2}$, not the difference $\Delta y_{i,t-2}$ [@arellano1989; @baltagi2021, p. 188] |
| γ is near one or $\sigma^2_\alpha$ dwarfs $\sigma^2_\varepsilon$ | Lagged levels are weak instruments for differences; difference GMM is biased and imprecise; consider system GMM [@baltagi2021, eqs. 8.34–8.35; @pesaran2015, p. 688] |
| System GMM is used | The initial-condition restriction is assumed; test the levels moments on their own, and expect the bias to grow with the variance ratio [@pesaran2015, p. 689; @croissant2019, p. 180; @bun2010; @baltagi2021, p. 202] |
| $m_1$ rejects and $m_2$ does not | The pattern the estimator needs [@baltagi2021, p. 192] |
| $m_2$ rejects | The innovations are serially correlated; the instruments dated $t - 2$ are invalid [@baltagi2021, p. 192; @croissant2019, p. 182] |
| The Sargan $p$-value is near one with many instruments | Not clean moments but the Bowsher pathology; cut the lags or collapse and test again [@baltagi2021, p. 192; @croissant2019, pp. 180–181] |
| Two-step estimates are reported | Report Windmeijer-corrected standard errors; the conventional ones are too small and the Wald tests oversized [@windmeijer2005; @baltagi2021, p. 193] |
| The instrument count approaches $N$ | The estimator drifts toward OLS; the coefficient that moves with the count is not a result [@croissant2019, p. 172; @baltagi2021, p. 194] |

## Next

[The error of a panel regression](../05-core/theory-panel-error.qmd)
covers serial correlation in the static error, the property the
$m$-tests above are built to check. The spatial half of a dynamic panel,
a lag in space as well as in time, has no estimator in R; the
[limits section](../03-spatial/index.qmd#sec-sp-dynamic) of the spatial
chapter says what that costs.

## Open

- **Ahn–Schmidt moments.** Under the standard assumptions there are
  $T - 2$ further conditions, $E(u_{iT}\Delta u_{it}) = 0$ for
  $t = 2, \dots, T-1$, nonlinear in the parameters, and with homoskedastic
  innovations $T - 1$ more; GMM on the full set is asymptotically efficient
  with the same asymptotic variance as maximum likelihood under normality
  [@ahn1995; @baltagi2021, eq. 8.26 and p. 201; @pesaran2015, eq. 27.36].
  Not in plm; `pdynmc` runs them [@fritsch2021], and the GMM step shows
  the fit in its pitfalls box.
- **Bias-corrected within.** @kiviet1995 approximates the within bias
  with exogenous regressors and subtracts a consistent estimate of it
  [@baltagi2021, p. 188; @pesaran2015, p. 680]; balanced panels only,
  and no endogenous regressors [@croissant2019, p. 166]. Not in R.
  Benchmark: Stata `xtlsdvc`, deferred.
- **Transformed likelihood.** @hsiao2002 difference the model, give the
  first difference $\Delta y_{i1}$ its own mean and variance, and maximise
  a likelihood in a fixed number of parameters; in their Monte Carlo it
  dominates GMM in small samples, at the price of cross-sectionally
  homoskedastic innovations [@pesaran2015, sec. 27.6, pp. 692–695]. Not in
  R. Benchmark: Stata `xtdpdqml` [@kripfganz2016; @baltagi2021, p. 197],
  deferred.
- **Time-invariant regressors.** Differencing removes them. @arellano1995
  recover them inside a Hausman–Taylor [@hausman1981] system, a
  random-effects IV estimator that uses the exogenous regressors as
  instruments, with a block-diagonal instrument matrix [@baltagi2021,
  sec. 8.3, pp. 194–198; @pesaran2015, sec. 27.4.4, pp. 686–687];
  @kripfganz2019 instead estimate the time-varying coefficients by GMM or
  quasi-maximum likelihood, regress the first-step residuals on the
  time-invariant regressors, and correct the second-step standard errors
  [@baltagi2021, pp. 197–198]. Not in R. Benchmark: Stata `xtseqreg`
  [@baltagi2021, p. 197], deferred.
- **Forward filtering.** The Keane–Runkle estimator removes a general
  serial correlation pattern by a Cholesky transform before two-stage
  least squares with predetermined instruments [@keane1992; @baltagi2021,
  sec. 8.6, p. 203; @pesaran2015, sec. 27.5, pp. 691–692]. Named only.
- **Errors that move together across firms.** A common unobserved factor
  in the innovations makes the GMM estimators above inconsistent; the
  short-$T$ answers are quasi-differencing GMM and a transformed
  quasi-likelihood [@pesaran2015, sec. 27.7, pp. 696–699]. Not in R.
